title: MAVEN: A Mesh-Aware Volumetric Encoding Network for Simulating 3D Flexible Deformation
primary_area: learning on graphs and other geometries & topologies

response.summary: MAVEN augments mesh simulators with explicit facet and cell nodes, geometry-aware vertex–element aggregation, facet-level contact, and cell–facet message passing. The approach is intuitive and produces strong rollout errors on two public datasets and one new elastoplastic bending dataset, but the central claim of robustness to sparse discretization is not directly isolated, and important architectural invariance and evaluation details remain unresolved.
strengths: The explicit joint modeling of vertices, facets, and volumetric cells is a useful, reasonably novel extension of conventional vertex-edge simulators, with a clear physical motivation for both contact and internal propagation (pp. 3–8).

MAVEN achieves the best reported full-rollout result for every quantity in Table 1, with particularly substantial gains on the coarse metal-bending task; three-run deviations and inference costs are also reported (pp. 9, 16–17).
Ablations separately examine learned geometric aggregation, explicit geometric inputs, and explicit higher-dimensional nodes, and show meaningful degradation when each is removed (pp. 9–10).
weaknesses: The headline sparse-mesh robustness claim is inferred by comparing different datasets rather than by systematically coarsening the same systems and testing resolution generalization. MBD is newly generated by the authors, while gains on the public DP benchmark are small, so evidence for the central claim is incomplete (pp. 8–10, 14–16).

The claimed permutation handling is technically questionable: vertices are concatenated after sorting by centroid distance, which is not unique for symmetric or regular facets/cells (e.g., cubes), and the learned joint weighting lacks a precise normalization definition. Rotation equivariance is also absent because global-frame relative vectors enter generic MLPs (pp. 6–7).

Baseline fairness and scope need strengthening: FIGNet is an author adaptation, hierarchical baselines use reduced hierarchies after their partitioner failed, contact radii are tuned only to equalize edge counts, and comparisons omit broader cellular/simplicial or hypergraph architectures. Generalization to unseen geometries, mesh qualities, resolutions, and material laws is not evaluated (pp. 9, 16, 18).
response.score_rationale: The method is promising and empirically competitive, but the evaluation does not directly establish its main robustness claim, while the ordering/invariance ambiguity affects technical soundness. These issues place it marginally below acceptance despite strong reported results.

response.summary: MAVEN represents cells, facets, and vertices in a heterogeneous mesh graph, using geometry-aware aggregation and facet-level contact modeling for autoregressive 3D deformation. Results are promising, especially on the new coarse elastoplastic bending task, but the evidence does not adequately isolate the paper’s central claim about robustness to sparse discretization.
strengths: The cell–facet–vertex construction is intuitive and practically relevant for volumetric deformation and contact, extending vertex-only simulators in a coherent architecture (pp. 4–7).
MAVEN achieves the best reported rollout errors across the evaluated quantities, with particularly substantial position gains on Metal Bending (p. 9).
Ablations separately support explicit element nodes, geometric features, and geometry-aware aggregation; runtime and parameter counts are also reported (pp. 10, 16–17).
weaknesses: The central sparse-mesh claim is not tested through controlled resolution sweeps on the same trajectories and physics. Instead, sparsity is inferred by comparing different datasets, while contact radii are separately tuned and baseline hierarchy depth is reduced because its partitioning failed (pp. 8–9, 16).

The claimed permutation handling is technically questionable: sorting vertices only by centroid distance is non-unique under common symmetric cells, while ordered concatenation feeds both aggregation-weight and contact encoders. Rotation equivariance/invariance is also not established for raw displacement vectors and normals processed by generic MLPs (pp. 6–7).

Evidence for physical fidelity is incomplete: evaluation relies mainly on averaged RMSE, without quantitative penetration/contact, conservation, stability, or out-of-distribution geometry/material tests. The new MBD dataset is simulator-generated and lacks independent validation, and mesh-quality sensitivity is acknowledged but not quantified (pp. 9, 14–18).
response.score_rationale: The approach is plausible and empirically encouraging, with useful ablations, but novelty appears incremental and decisive validation of sparse-mesh/contact robustness is missing. Ambiguities in ordering and geometric invariance further weaken technical confidence. I therefore rate it marginally below acceptance; uncertainty remains because code and supplementary animations are unavailable.

response.summary: MAVEN augments mesh simulators with explicit vertex, facet, and cell representations, using geometry-aware aggregation and cell–facet message passing for 3D deformation and contact. The approach is practically motivated and performs well on three datasets, especially the coarse-mesh metal-bending task, but technical invariance issues and incomplete evidence for the central sparse-mesh claim keep it marginally below acceptance.
strengths: The explicit treatment of facets for contact and cells for volumetric propagation is intuitive and constitutes a meaningful architectural extension beyond the evaluated vertex-only models (pp. 4–8).

MAVEN achieves the best reported rollout errors across all quantities, with particularly substantial position gains on cavity grasping and metal bending; repeated-run deviations and comparable parameter budgets are provided (pp. 9, 16).
Ablations separately support explicit higher-dimensional nodes, geometric inputs, and geometry-aware aggregation, while runtime remains close to other flat graph models (pp. 9–10, 17).
weaknesses: The claimed permutation invariance is not technically established: vertices are concatenated after sorting only by distance to the centroid (pp. 6–7), which is non-unique for symmetric or regular facets/cells. Face features likewise concatenate ordered per-vertex vectors, and rotation/reflection behavior is not analyzed.

The core claim of robustness to sparse discretization lacks a controlled mesh-resolution study on the same physical problems. The evidence instead compares different datasets with different meshes, and the admitted marked degradation on low-quality meshes is not quantified (pp. 8–10, 18).

Novelty is insufficiently positioned relative to general cellular, simplicial, hypergraph, or incidence-based neural networks. Empirically, only three tasks are tested, one internally generated; hierarchical baselines are modified because their partitioning fails, and there are no out-of-distribution, conservation/stability, or long-horizon failure analyses (pp. 8–9, 14–16).
response.score_rationale: The facet–cell representation is promising and the reported gains are credible enough to warrant interest. However, an incorrect or incomplete invariance construction, limited novelty positioning, and the absence of controlled sparsity and robustness experiments leave central claims insufficiently validated for acceptance.

response.summary: MAVEN augments mesh simulators with explicit cell and facet nodes, geometry-derived features, facet-level contact, and cell–facet message passing. This is a sensible, moderately novel architectural direction, and the reported results are promising, especially on the coarse proprietary metal-bending task. However, the central coarse-mesh claim is not isolated experimentally, and important invariance and reproducibility issues weaken the evidence.
strengths: Explicitly representing vertices, facets, and volumetric cells is well motivated for deformation and contact, and the resulting cell–facet architecture is clearly differentiated from vertex-only GNNs (pp. 3–8).

MAVEN achieves the best reported aggregate errors across three datasets and multiple quantities, with particularly substantial gains on metal bending; three-run deviations and comparable parameter budgets are provided (pp. 9, 16).
Ablations separately support explicit element nodes, geometric features, and geometry-aware aggregation, while runtime remains reasonably close to other learned models (pp. 9–10, 17).
weaknesses: The claimed permutation invariance is technically questionable: sorting vertices by distance to an element centroid does not define a unique order for symmetric regular cells/facets, where ties are common. Moreover, raw relative vectors and normals passed through generic MLPs provide translation equivariance but no demonstrated rotation equivariance or robustness (pp. 6–7).

The main claim concerns stability under sparse discretization, yet there is no controlled mesh-resolution sweep on fixed physics/geometries. The strongest gains come from the newly generated MBD dataset, while gains on the dense public DP dataset are small, and the appendix explicitly reports marked sensitivity to mesh quality without quantitative results (pp. 9, 14–16, 18).

Experimental comparability and reproducibility are incomplete: contact radii are dataset-specific and chosen to equalize edge counts rather than contact fidelity; FIGNet is adapted, and hierarchy depth is reduced because subdivision failed. There are no tests of unseen orientations, mesh topologies/resolutions, conservation or penetration metrics, or comparisons against recent cell-complex/hypergraph formulations (pp. 8–9, 16–18).
response.score_rationale: The paper contains a useful geometric inductive bias and encouraging empirical gains, but the novelty is incremental over face-aware and higher-order graph ideas, while the invalid/underspecified ordering invariance and lack of controlled sparsity/generalization studies leave the central claims insufficiently established. I therefore rate it marginally below acceptance; uncertainty remains because code and supplementary animations are unavailable in the supplied material.

response.summary: MAVEN augments mesh simulators with explicit cell and facet nodes, geometry-aware vertex–element mappings, and facet-level contact. The idea is relevant and results are promising, especially on coarse contact simulation, but key invariance claims and the evidence for robustness under sparse discretization are insufficiently established.
strengths: Explicitly representing volumetric cells and boundary facets is a sensible extension beyond vertex-only simulators, with a clear motivation for coarse-mesh contact (pp. 2–8).
MAVEN achieves the best reported aggregate errors across three datasets under broadly similar parameter budgets, with particularly large position gains on the new metal-bending task (pp. 9, 16).
Ablations separately test learned geometric aggregation, explicit geometric features, and higher-dimensional nodes, and all materially improve the difficult coarse-mesh setting (pp. 9–10).
weaknesses: The claimed permutation invariance is not technically justified: sorting vertices only by distance to the centroid is non-unique for symmetric regular cells and facets, while concatenation-based MLPs in Eqs. 3 and 6 remain ordering-sensitive. Handling tetrahedra versus hexahedra and variable facet arities is also underspecified (pp. 6–7).

The central sparse-mesh claim lacks controlled resolution or mesh-quality sweeps, out-of-distribution discretization tests, and quantitative contact/interpenetration metrics. The strongest gains come from the authors' own dataset, while the public deforming-plate gains are modest (pp. 9–10, 17–18).

Reproducibility and comparison fairness are limited: the new dataset omits important Abaqus/contact details, and its ellipse specification independently samples c/a and b/a despite their required geometric relation; hierarchical baselines are modified because partitioning failed, and only three training runs are reported (pp. 15–16).
response.score_rationale: The cell–facet formulation is useful and empirically promising, but its novelty is incremental and the current presentation leaves a material invariance flaw plus insufficient evidence for the headline coarse-mesh robustness claim. These issues place the work marginally below acceptance, though clarification and controlled mesh-resolution experiments could change the assessment.
